📚 Today you learned

Merger Arbitrage — Trading the Deal Spread

RMCF jumped 163% today on an 8-K saying the board is "considering" a sale after receiving buyout interest — no signed deal, no fixed price, no closing date. That's speculative buyout chatter, not merger arbitrage. Real merger arb starts only after a definitive agreement is signed at a stated price (say, $20/share cash): the stock then trades at a small discount to $20 (the "spread") reflecting the risk the deal falls through or gets delayed, and arbitrageurs buy the stock and collect that spread as the deal closes. The discipline is knowing which stage you're in. Pre-deal rumors like RMCF's are binary and can round-trip to zero on no news at all — there's no fixed price anchoring the downside. Post-signing arb has a real price anchor and a knowable catalyst (shareholder vote, regulatory clearance), which is why professional arb desks won't touch a stock until the definitive agreement exists.

Also today: Deal break risk — the chance a signed merger falls apart (financing, antitrust, shareholder vote) before closing; this is what the arb spread is actually pricing.
